## 1. A: Social protection (pensions, benefits and social care)

Spending page: of every £100 spent on services, the largest share, £33, went on social protection. Health was next with £21.

Where the site says it:

- `spending.html`: "the largest share, £33, went on social protection"
- `spending.html`: "Health was next with £21"

## 2. C: Income Tax, National Insurance and VAT

Taxes page: Income Tax (£329bn), National Insurance (£204bn) and VAT (£180bn) raised 65% of all tax.

Where the site says it:

- `taxes.html`: "Three taxes raised 65% of all tax: Income Tax (£329bn), National Insurance (£204bn) and VAT (£180bn)"

## 3. D: The gap between what was spent and what came in, which adds to the national debt

Taxes page: borrowing is not income from tax; it is the gap between spending and receipts, and it adds to the national debt. Debt (the total owed) is a different number, £2,917bn.

Where the site says it:

- `taxes.html`: "Borrowing is not income from tax. It is the gap between spending"
- `taxes.html`: "and it adds to the national debt"

## 4. C: About 27%

Who pays page: the top 1% of Income Tax payers paid 27.2% of all Income Tax. 59.1% is the top 10%.

Where the site says it:

- `who-pays.html`: "the top 1% of Income Tax payers paid 27.2% of all Income Tax"

## 5. A: It is an average across households, counting all taxes, and it is not the tax rate any one person pays

Tax and income page, 'Three numbers that are easy to mix up': 33.6% is an average across all people using their household's income and taxes. It is not the tax rate any one person pays, and it is not a share of all tax raised.

Where the site says it:

- `household-tax.html`: "taxes took 33.6% of gross household income in 2023/24"
- `household-tax.html`: "It is not the tax rate any one person pays"
- `index.html`: "That is an average across households, not anyone's tax rate"

## 6. B: Taxes on spending, such as VAT

Tax and income page: for people in the lowest-income fifth, most of their household's tax is indirect (taxes on spending), 21.0% of gross household income.

Where the site says it:

## 7. D: A made-up example that shows how the tax rules work, not a measured figure

## 8. B: About the same

Year by year, Earnings: £767 a week in April 2025, about the same as April 2021 (£761 in April 2025 prices). Before allowing for prices it rose from £610, about a quarter, which is why A is wrong. Pay is compared from 2021 because the survey changed how it codes jobs in 2011 and 2021.

Where the site says it:

- `life/earnings.html`: "pay in April 2025 was about the same as in April 2021"

## 12. D: Nothing: the figures show what changed, not why

Every year and comparison page says 'Change is not cause': the figures show what changed between years, not why, and they cannot separate the economy, prices, population and government policy.
